item.title: Every measure of crypto usage rose this week and no price followed
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Crypto cards at $759 million a month, Hyperliquid burning $175 million of fees, and an $91.3 billion study that found zero institutional buyers of tokenised assets.
item.content:encoded:
Crypto cards at $759 million a month, Hyperliquid burning $175 million of fees, and an $91.3 billion study that found zero institutional buyers of tokenised assets.

The single most repeated finding on this channel since the split is not a price call. It is a gap. In four of five editions the same thing happened from a different angle: something measurable about crypto adoption went up and the tokens did not.

That divergence is now large enough, and specific enough, to be the week's subject rather than a recurring aside. This memo is about whether it closes, and what has to be true for it to.

The evidence, gathered in one place

What roseBy how much
Crypto payment card volume$759 million in July, 2.5x from $306 million a year earlier, from under $1 million in October 2023
Hyperliquid fees, Q2about $175 million, 80 percent from perpetuals, buying and burning the token
Solana tokenised equity volume$1 million in June 2025 to over $3 billion in June 2026
Robinhood Chain, seven-day DEX volumenearly $3 billion, with perpetuals up 130 percent
Tokenised RWA deposits$2.3 billion to $7.4 billion
Tokenised stock holders1.2 million, up 1,406.8 percent in a year
BlackRock tokenised products on Ethereumtwo funds, then twelve more announced days later
JP Morgan's Kinexysroughly $5 billion a day, with a collateral fund nearing $1 billion on public Ethereum

Against all of that: Bitcoin sits near $64,800, roughly 49 percent below its October high of $126,198. Ether is near $1,906, from almost $5,000 six months ago. Tokens broadly are at 2026 lows, about 40 percent off the May peak. Bitcoin volatility is at three-year lows and 23 percent of the top miners are running at a daily loss.

Two years of adoption compounding and the asset prices went backwards.

1. The bull case: this is a lag, and lags close

The revenue actually inflected, and that is datable. Per Milk Road, a Bitwise analyst puts the trough in network revenue between late 2025 and early 2026, with revenue rising since while prices kept falling. That is not a narrative claim, it is a series with a turn in it.

Some of it accrues directly. Hyperliquid's roughly $175 million of quarterly fees, 80 percent of them from perpetuals, buys and burns HYPE. Pons on Robinhood Chain routes about 80 percent of receipts into buybacks and burns and has already retired 24 percent of its supply. Where the mechanism exists, the cash flow reaches the token.

Ether has a genuinely new demand source for the first time in a year. Robinhood's chain has no token of its own, so transactions on it consume Ether, and a large portion of the supply has already been bridged there. That is roughly 30 million users generating base-layer demand by construction rather than by speculation.

The institutional pipe is being built by the people who matter. Per the Milk Road Show, BlackRock did not tokenise two funds and stop, it announced twelve more within days. JP Morgan is running $5 billion a day through Kinexys and has a collateral money market fund approaching $1 billion on public Ethereum. Ethereum holds 52.2 percent of tokenised real-world asset market capitalisation and 69.4 percent of euro stablecoin supply.

And the desk that gets paid to be right is buying. Per DeFi Dad's interview, Fundstrat's Sean Farrell puts us at "the seventh inning stretch, maybe even later in the game" and says plainly: "you could buy the majors right now... and sell them at a higher price, say a year from now."

2. The bear case: none of it has to accrue to a token, and mostly it does not

The card business is the cleanest example and it is damning. Per a16z crypto, $759 million a month, growing 2.5 times a year, nearly 9 million purchases at about $86 each. Settlement is 58 percent USDC and 26 percent USDT, with euro stablecoins collapsing from 88 percent of volume to 2. And it runs almost entirely over Visa. That is a payment rail compounding beautifully in digital dollars, and there is no token anywhere in the value chain. Stablecoin adoption is not crypto-asset adoption.

The tokenisation buyers are crypto itself. This is the number of the week. An Arrakis study carried by Blockworks of $91.3 billion of on-chain acquisitions across ten tokenised dollar-yield products found two thirds came from protocol and DAO treasuries and not one dollar traced to a traditional bank, pension fund or asset manager. Wallets above $1 million were 4 percent of buyers and 93 percent of the capital.

So the plumbing is being laid by BlackRock and JP Morgan, and the volume through it is crypto recycling its own treasury cash. Both halves of that sentence are true, and the second one is the one that decides prices.

Ethereum's own architecture leaks the value. Per 0xSammy and the Ethereum Institutional founders, Robinhood's layer two brought roughly 30 million users and sends the base chain "a couple of thousand dollars" in fees. Joe Lubin's stated position is growth over rent extraction. That is defensible for a network and terrible for an asset. Vitalik's Lean Ethereum roadmap then targets a tenfold fee reduction, a bear case for accrual before it is a bull case for adoption.

Coinbase's own AI lead conceded the point. Asked whether agentic payment demand accrues value to tokens, the answer was that block space is commoditised and agentic payments could run on a parallel chain. The host called it an extremely controversial answer. It is also probably the correct one.

And the forced sellers are still there. Farrell names them: miners selling to fund capex, holders on the four-year cycle, treasury companies unable to raise below one times net asset value and now selling, and redemptions from liquid funds. The real two-year yield is at a cycle high. That is the liquidity condition that has to change first.

3. The arbitration

Both cases are correct about different things, so the resolution is not "which one wins" but "which assets are on which side of the line."

The divergence closes for assets with a fee-to-token mechanism and does not close for the rest. Hyperliquid has one. Pons has one. Ether has a partial one that its own roadmap is about to weaken. Bitcoin has none and never claimed to. That is why usage data was never going to move it.

The honest weakness in the bull case is the resolution condition. Asked when the gap closes, the Bitwise answer was "when people start understanding what's going on on chain," with no date, no target and no flow number attached. A fundamentals case with no catalyst is a reason to own something, not a reason to expect it to move.

I am 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000, unchanged. Two independent frameworks put the cycle low in the fourth quarter: Benjamin Cowen has us on day 1,354 against prior bottoms at 1,432 and 1,436, and day 304 against an average bear bottom on day 406, with October as base case. Trader Mayne puts the bottoming range at $40,000 to $60,000. Farrell's bear case is a four handle. My number sits between credible desks rather than outside them.

On Ether I am 60/40 with CryptoKaleo's one-more-leg-down against Arthur Hayes calling $5,000 by year end, for the accrual reason above rather than an adoption one.

What to do with it

Separate the two trades and stop calling them one sector. Owning Bitcoin is a liquidity and debasement position. Owning a fee-burning protocol is an equity-like cash-flow position. This week they diverged and they will keep diverging.

If you want the adoption theme, the honest expression is the equity, not the token. The card volume runs over Visa. The tokenisation plumbing runs through BlackRock and JP Morgan. The retail bid runs through Robinhood, whose event contracts now out-earn both its equities and its crypto lines.

Watchlist for the week ahead. $BTC into a fourth-quarter low that three independent clocks agree on. $ETH, where the institutional case and the accrual case point opposite ways and Glamsterdam lands in the third quarter. $HYPE as the cleanest fee-to-token mechanism in the market, with 433,025 coins just unlocked against the burn. $HOOD, where the chain is the funnel and the brokerage is the business. And $MSTR, which Farrell names as the sector's tail risk through its putable bond repurchases.

The scoreboard, Bitcoin & Crypto

This is the youngest book of the three and the record reflects that.

ResolvedOutcome
Robinhood Chain holds $400 million a day of DEX volume by August 10, aixbtHit, four days early. Seven-day volume ran near $3 billion, roughly $428 million a day
ERCOT's Batch Zero round stays frozen under the Texas audit, m0xtHit. The round came due August 7 and did not advance

Two settled calls, both hits, and both are other people's. Zero house calls have resolved on this channel. There is no hit rate to report and quoting 100 percent off two relayed calls would be advertising rather than scorekeeping, so the honest line is that this book has not been tested yet.

Fifty-five open calls carried into next week. The ones that carry the argument above: Bitcoin at $58,000 before $75,000 at 60/40. CLARITY's failure already priced at 65/35, which this week supported when the bill died and Bitcoin rose the same afternoon. Ether at 60/40 for one more leg down. The on-chain revenue divergence itself. The Arrakis finding that no institution has bought a tokenised asset. Crypto card adoption at $759 million a month. Galaxy landing a Helios tenant before the Texas audit clears. And Tilman Holloway's call that Coldcard drives ETF inflows three, six and nine months out. That one has the longest fuse and the cleanest test.

item.title: Crypto cards hit $759 million a month while the tokens did nothing
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Fundstrat's Sean Farrell says buy the majors now and names a four-handle Bitcoin as his bear case, and CLARITY's earliest procedural vote is September 15.
item.content:encoded:
Fundstrat's Sean Farrell says buy the majors now and names a four-handle Bitcoin as his bear case, and CLARITY's earliest procedural vote is September 15.

Yesterday the bill died and Bitcoin went up. All week the same pattern held in miniature. Every measure of actual usage rose, and no price followed any of it.

Market context. Bitcoin sits near $64,800, derived from a 1,346 coin transfer out of Galaxy Digital worth $87.28 million on the Crypto list. Ether is near $1,906, from a whale who capitulated after three years, selling 7,323 coins for $13.96 million against a $2,723 average entry and more than $19 million of realised losses.

Tom Lee's framing of that is the week in one line: "6 months ago Ethereum was almost $5,000. Now it's $1,800. Has anything really changed? Not really."

The institutional bid is still there and still quiet. BlackRock's fund took $604 million over four days, and per Lark Davis Larry Fink's public read is that crypto had too much leverage, got washed out, and there is more stability at these levels. Underneath, Bitcoin volatility is at three-year lows and, per the Kalshi list, 23 percent of the top miners are running at a daily loss.

1. On-chain revenue inflected months ago and the prices never noticed. Per Milk Road, a Bitwise on-chain analyst puts the trough in network revenue at "between end of 2025 early 2026," with revenue picking up since while tokens kept falling.

The specifics are not small.

On-chainFigure
Hyperliquid fees, Q2 2026about $175 million, 80 percent from perpetuals, buying and burning HYPE
Solana tokenised equity volume$1 million in June 2025 to more than $3 billion in June 2026
Avalanchetransactions quadrupled on an RWA pivot, with FIFA running its own chain
Progmat, Japan's largest tokenisation platformbringing more than $2 billion of assets

The honest weakness is the resolution condition. Asked when the divergence closes, the answer is "when people start understanding what's going on on chain," with no date, no target and no flow number attached. A fundamentals case with no catalyst is a reason to own something, not a reason to expect it to move.

2. Crypto cards are the adoption number nobody quotes, and they are almost entirely Visa. Per a16z crypto, monthly crypto payment card volume reached $759 million in July, up roughly 2.5 times from $306 million a year earlier, and up from less than $1 million when tracking began in October 2023. Purchases hit nearly 9 million in July against 5.2 million a year ago, at an average of about $86 a transaction.

The composition shift is the real finding. Dollar stablecoins took the market: USDC now handles about 58 percent of card spending and USDT about 26, from roughly 48 and 7 a year ago. Euro-backed stablecoins went from 88 percent of volume in early 2024 to about 2 percent. Settlement moved with it, from Gnosis dominance to Optimism at 29 percent, Solana and Base at about 19 each, with Gnosis down to 2.

This is what adoption looks like when it stops being a narrative: a payment rail growing 2.5 times a year, denominated in digital dollars, running almost entirely over Visa. None of it accrues to a token. That is precisely why it has not shown up in a price.

3. Fundstrat says buy the majors and puts the bear case at a four handle. Per DeFi Dad's interview with Sean Farrell, Fundstrat's head of digital asset strategy is unambiguous about where we are: "we are in the throes of a bear market... if I had to put an inning on it, I would say that we are in the seventh inning stretch. Uh maybe maybe even later in the game."

His call is the only named allocation decision anyone made this week. "I feel pretty comfortable that you could buy the majors right now... I'm pretty sure you could buy the majors and sell them at a higher price, say a year from now." He is more patient on alts, because the ones he likes have already bounced 25 to 50 percent off the lows.

The bear case he asks clients to stomach is "a forehand on Bitcoin," meaning a $40,000s print. That sits below Mike Novogratz's $60,000 to $80,000 base case and well below the $72,000 level where BitcoinJesusETH expects a relief rally to fail.

His diagnosis of why is the useful part. Crypto is "an excess liquidity sponge" and there has been no excess liquidity, so marginal capital went to assets producing earnings. The forced sellers are named: miners selling to fund capex, holders on the four-year cycle, treasury companies unable to raise below one times net asset value and now selling, and redemptions from liquid funds. The real two-year yield is at a new cycle high.

I am holding 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. Farrell's four handle is more bearish than my call and Novogratz's floor is above it, so my number sits between two credible desks rather than outside them. What would change it is the liquidity condition Farrell names, and nothing next week supplies it.

4. Two handicappers disagree on CLARITY and both say it stopped mattering. The earliest procedural vote is now September 15. Per Jordi Visser, the odds fell from 40 percent to 17 and he calls it "officially being quote unquote done for this year." Farrell is the other side, "above a coin flip" that a compromise on the ethics provision lands, and says that absent that provision he would be at 100 percent.

They agree on the thing that matters. SEC and CFTC rules arrive regardless and are, in Farrell's words, "pretty aligned with what Clarity says."

That is the case for my 65/35 that the failure is already priced, and this week supported it. Bitcoin rose on the delay. What the two of them also expose is the real gating item, and it is not policy substance: the hold-up is Trump's own crypto earnings and the ethics language written to cover them.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Near $64,800 with volatility at three-year lows and $604 million of BlackRock buying over four sessions. Farrell says buy the majors here for a one-year hold and warns you may see a four handle first. Both can be true, and position size is the only thing that reconciles them.
  • $ETH. Down from almost $5,000 six months ago to about $1,900, with a three-year holder capitulating into it. Farrell calls it "one of the most clean macro trades of the next cycle." Robinhood's chain has no token, so its transactions consume Ether. That is the first genuine new demand source in a year.
  • $HYPE. About $175 million of second-quarter fees with 80 percent from perpetuals, all of it buying and burning the token. HyperLabs unlocked another 433,025 coins worth $23.46 million this week, so supply is arriving alongside the burn.
  • $MSTR. Farrell names it as the sector's tail risk, specifically the putable bond repurchases that spiralled through the preferred and the broader complex. The company is deleveraging in public and the market is still deciding whether that was a choice.
  • $HOOD. Per the Financial Markets list, it formed a golden cross for the first time since January 2024, and the last one preceded a 440 percent run over thirteen months. Its chain is where the only live retail bid in crypto actually sits, even though the coins are now the loss leader against event contracts.

item.title: CLARITY died and Bitcoin reclaimed $65,000 the same afternoon
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The Senate punted the vote to September, Kalshi's odds of it becoming law this year hit an all-time low of 16 percent, and BlackRock bought 9,269 coins over four straight days anyway.
item.content:encoded:
The Senate punted the vote to September, Kalshi's odds of it becoming law this year hit an all-time low of 16 percent, and BlackRock bought 9,269 coins over four straight days anyway.

Yesterday a hundred million dollars walked out of self-custody wallets and Bitcoin did not move. Today the bill this sector spent a year lobbying for died, and Bitcoin went up. Two days, one answer.

Market context. Per the Kalshi list, Bitcoin reclaimed $65,000 on the day the CLARITY vote slipped, roughly half its October high. Per the Crypto list, the bid behind it is institutional and it is not subtle: BlackRock logged four consecutive days of net inflows totalling 9,269 Bitcoin, about $604 million, with Morgan Stanley buying three days running and Bhutan selling $27 million into it.

The rest of the tape is flat to soft. Per Blockworks, ETF flows overall are still anemic, and the 60-day correlation between Bitcoin and Ether ETF flows has climbed to plus 0.67, so the two move as one allocation now rather than two decisions. Miners are distributing, MARA and Riot sending a combined 581 coins to NYDIG, and the proxies split on earnings rather than beta, Galaxy up 3.6 percent and Circle up 3.1 percent against an index down 1.1.

The scoreboard.

  • Working, and the delay is the proof. On Thursday I went 65/35 that CLARITY's failure was already priced. The Senate punted it, Kalshi's odds of passage this year hit 16 percent, an all-time low, and Bitcoin closed higher on the news.
  • Strengthened. My 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. Benjamin Cowen's cycle arithmetic now puts us three quarters through the bear with the low still ahead.
  • Due today, and it did not clear. ERCOT's Batch Zero study round stayed suspended under the Texas audit, so Galaxy's approved megawatts keep their scarcity value and its uncontracted pipeline keeps waiting.
  • Standing. The 60/40 that Galaxy lands a Helios tenant before the audit clears. Still no announcement.

1. The catalyst everyone was hedging died, and the hedge paid nothing. Macro has the vote math tonight: cloture never filed, Senate back September 14. What matters here is the price reaction, and there was not one. Traders had spent the week positioning for the opposite. Per Trader Mayne, CryptoFace was building a straddle into the vote on the view that a failure delivers "that one leg down." It did not arrive.

The reason is that the market had already marked the bill down to nothing. Michael Saylor's line, carried on the Kalshi list, is the framing that fits: "Bitcoin doesn't need CLARITY. America needs clarity." BitQua put the trader's version of it better: "The most bullish outcome for bitcoin is not necessarily a particular answer, it's getting an answer. Just, yes or no." A punt is the one outcome that resolves nothing, and Bitcoin rose anyway.

I am holding 65/35 and adding a leg: the unpriced risk sits in the alt market rather than in Bitcoin, because Coinbase has already said it keeps expanding offshore if the bill fails. Haseeb Qureshi, on the Crypto list, is the counterweight, noting Kalshi still prices better than 30 percent for next year and above 50 percent by 2028. Late is not dead.

2. Cowen has us on day 1,354 of a cycle that bottoms around day 1,435. Per Benjamin Cowen, the arithmetic is unusually clean.

Cycle positionReading
Days since the last low1,354, against bottoms at 1,432 and 1,436
Days since the peak304, against an average bear bottom on day 406
Moving averageslost the 50-week, lost the 100-week, now at the 200-week
His windowlate September to mid December, base case October

His verdict on whether the low is in: "Doubtful that it started yet, we could still go a little bit lower." He has been buying below 60,000 and says he got wrecked six months after doing the same in 2018 and 2022, and did not care six months after that.

Trader Mayne lands in the same place from a different angle, putting the bottoming range at 40,000 to 60,000 with a weekly market structure break as the trigger rather than a price. Two independent frameworks, no shared method, same fourth-quarter answer. This is the strongest support my 60/40 has had.

3. Ethereum won the institutions and the token collects nothing. Per the Milk Road Show with the three founders of Ethereum Institutional, the pipe is real. BlackRock tokenised two funds on Ethereum this week and announced twelve more products days later. JP Morgan's Kinexys runs roughly $5 billion a day, and its JLTXX collateral fund sits on public Ethereum approaching $1 billion. Ethereum holds 52.2 percent of tokenised real-world asset market capitalisation and 69.4 percent of euro stablecoin supply.

Now the part that decides whether any of it is investable. Robinhood's chain is an Ethereum layer two that brought roughly 30 million users, and the fees reaching Ethereum from it are "a couple of thousand dollars right now." Joe Lubin's stated position is growth over rent extraction. That is a defensible strategy for the network and a terrible one for the asset.

Vitalik's answer is the Lean Ethereum roadmap, per Lark Davis: recursive proofs so a validator runs on a phone, post-quantum cryptography by 2028 or 2029, and a state redesign targeting a tenfold fee reduction. Glamsterdam lands in the third quarter.

So the desks split. Per the Crypto list, Arthur Hayes wants $5,000 Ether by year end. CryptoKaleo sees "one last leg down." I am 60/40 with Kaleo into the fourth quarter, because a ten times fee cut is a bear case for accrual before it is a bull case for adoption.

4. Nobody has bought a tokenised asset except crypto itself. The most damning number of the week came out of an Arrakis study carried by Blockworks. Across $91.3 billion of on-chain acquisitions of ten tokenised dollar-yield products, two thirds came from protocol and DAO treasuries, and not one dollar traced to a traditional bank, pension fund or asset manager. Wallets above $1 million were 4 percent of buyers and 93 percent of the capital.

Set that against the institutional pipe above and the picture resolves. The plumbing is being built by BlackRock and JP Morgan. The volume through it is crypto recycling its own treasury cash.

Retail rotated rather than left. July gacha spend fell to $290.3 million from June's record $354.8 million while Pump.fun's daily average rose 21 percent.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Reclaimed $65,000 on a dead legislative catalyst, with $604 million of BlackRock buying behind it over four sessions. Cowen and Mayne independently put the low in the fourth quarter, so treat strength as a bear-market rally until a weekly structure break says otherwise.
  • $ETH. The institutional adoption is genuine and the fee accrual is not. Glamsterdam in the third quarter cuts fees another order of magnitude. Hayes wants $5,000 and Kaleo wants one more flush, and the roadmap argues for Kaleo first.
  • $HOOD. Event contracts brought in $156 million against $129 million from equities and $100 million from crypto, up more than tenfold on 13.6 billion contracts, while crypto revenue fell 38 percent and app volume dropped 35 percent. The prediction market is the business now and the coins are the loss leader.
  • $GLXY. Up 3.6 percent on the quarter while the sector fell, still with no Helios tenant and ERCOT's Batch Zero round frozen. Every week the queue stays shut, its approved megawatts get scarcer and its uncontracted pipeline gets cheaper.
  • $MSTR. Built an all-time-high dollar reserve covering 2.3 years of dividends and interest, and Saylor is marketing STRC's 11.5 percent tax-deferred yield as the equivalent of an 18 percent bank account for a Miami taxpayer. The yield pitch is what replaces the coin-buying story.

item.title: $100 million walked out of Coldcard wallets and Bitcoin moved less than one percent
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: A random-number bug from 2021 left older seeds guessable, more than 5,000 holders lost coins, and the only thing in crypto that reacted was Robinhood's memecoin chain.
item.content:encoded:
A random-number bug from 2021 left older seeds guessable, more than 5,000 holders lost coins, and the only thing in crypto that reacted was Robinhood's memecoin chain.

Yesterday Galaxy proved the miners had stopped being a Bitcoin trade. Today a hundred million dollars walked out of self-custody wallets and the price barely registered it. Nothing moves this asset anymore, and that is the read.

Market context. Per Milk Road, Bitcoin topped at $126,198 last October and sits roughly 49 percent below it this afternoon. Per VirtualBacon, it is up 3.6 percent over four days and still in a daily downtrend that began in May, with resistance at 66.7K and a break opening 76K. It sits on its 200-week average, the level that marked every prior cycle floor.

Benjamin Cowen's framing on NFA Live is the one to carry: Bitcoin sits at the same valuation against the S&P 500 as five to six years ago, while the S&P makes new highs. Per Blockworks, ETF net flows are anemic in both directions and Glassnode has options priced for no move. Miners were the worst asset on the board at minus 6.2 percent, with Cipher and Hut 8 both missing.

The scoreboard.

  • Hit, four days early. On July 11 I said Robinhood Chain had to hold $400 million a day of DEX volume by August 10 or the migration was churn. Seven-day volume is near $3 billion, roughly $428 million a day. It cleared.
  • Working. My 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. Three independent clocks now point at a low between October and December, and none point up first.
  • Called it, and it cost 13 percent. I said yesterday Galaxy's 830 approved megawatts needed a tenant within days. Novogratz had promised one by the end of summer and did not deliver.
  • Due tomorrow. ERCOT's next Batch Zero round, which the Texas audit suspended.

1. The Coldcard bug was born in 2021, and the coins left this week. Per Swan, a 2021 software integration made Coldcard seed generation fall through to a MicroPython pseudo-random number generator instead of the hardware entropy source it was meant to use. Coinkite puts affected MK2 and MK3 seeds at roughly 40 bits of effective search space, with MK4, MK5 and Q near 72 bits. The design target was 128.

Forty bits is not a lock somebody picked. It is a lock with a thousand keys.

Per the People to follow list, one researcher mapped 4,312 drained addresses with the exact block for each. Per Anthony Pompliano's guests, the total is more than 5,000 people and over $100 million, concentrated among the holders least likely to ever use a custodian. Bitcoin did not move more than about one percent on it.

The position is not a price call. Tilman Holloway expects ETF inflows to tick up three, six and nine months out as burned self-custody holders move to a custodian, against Coinbase and BitGo carrying roughly $5 million of insurance. The remedy circulating on Spaces is generating your own entropy with 100 dice rolls. That tells you how this ends.

The most damning line came from calle on the Crypto list: "not a single vulnerability was found by a US frontier model. Instead, we're spending $10k a day on open weights models like Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 to find vulnerabilities in Bitcoin infrastructure."

2. CLARITY's death is a buy-the-news event, and I am taking the unpopular side. Macro has the vote math tonight: 60 needed, 53 held, cloture filed on a different motion. Here it is a straight disagreement between desks. Per VirtualBacon, Bernstein says failure could trigger the final leg down in crypto valuations and JPMorgan calls it another headwind. Bitwise's Matt Hougan says the SEC and CFTC can supply the same path by rule rather than law. Altcoin Daily puts a failure at Bitcoin "maybe into the 50s, maybe into 48."

James Seyffart's point decides it. Traditional finance treats CLARITY as a catalyst for Bitcoin, not only for alts, so the disappointment is broad rather than confined to tokens that need a legal wrapper.

I am 65/35 that it is already priced. Polymarket went from 50 to 70 percent in January to 15 percent now, and an asset that ignored a $100 million theft is not holding a legislative premium. Hougan is the reason I lean that way. A rulemaking path does not need 60 votes.

3. Galaxy's missing tenant cost it 13 percent, and the frozen queue is why waiting is correct. Per Milk Road, $GLXY fell 13 percent to $19 on a $7.5 billion market cap, and none of it was the numbers. Helios phase one, 200 megawatts leased to CoreWeave for 15 years, is billing toward roughly $80 million a quarter.

Per m0xt on the Stocks list, the pipeline is 5.7 gigawatts with 4.3 contracted, contractable or Batch Zero eligible, and the Texas audit ordered August 3 suspended the next Batch Zero round, due tomorrow. Merlin's first phase is 74 megawatts, one under the 75 megawatt threshold that would have caught it. Caspian at 700 and Selene at 900 are grandfathered.

So the moat held and the announcement did not. I am 60/40 the tenant lands before the audit clears, because a landlord with grandfathered megawatts inside a frozen queue has the only product anyone can plug in.

4. The only live bid in crypto is on Robinhood's chain, and none of it is Bitcoin. Per 0xSammy, Robinhood Chain carries $411 million of DeFi value, $558 million of stablecoins, over $1 billion bridged and nearly $3 billion of seven-day DEX volume, with perpetual futures up 130 percent.

The economics are the interesting part. Apps on the chain took $1.6 million of gross fees in 24 hours and the chain kept $50 thousand. Fat apps, thin chain, no token to dilute. Pons alone runs 64 percent of launchpad volume on a $20 million market cap, and Uniswap has now deployed pools.trade on the same chain to take it.

The other half of the flow is real-world assets, compounding while everything crypto-native shrinks.

On-chainA year agoNow
RWA deposits$2.3 billion$7.4 billion
RWA perpetual notional, July$1.3 billion$150 billion
Tokenized spot volume, monthly$3.4 billion$14 billion

Crypto-native spot DEX volume fell about 70 percent over the same stretch. That is where the money went. Not out of the sector, sideways within it.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Roughly 49 percent below October's $126,198 and resting on the 200-week average, with 66.7K the line that matters. Three bottom clocks (Cowen's capitulation event, the 13-month underwater cohort, Altcoin Daily's 200-week analogue) all land in the fourth quarter, none starting with a rally.
  • $GLXY. Down 13 percent for the absence of an announcement rather than a number, while its 830 approved megawatts got scarcer. Tomorrow's suspended Batch Zero round is the next marker.
  • $HOOD. Its chain does $3 billion a week in DEX volume and keeps almost none of the fees. That is deliberate: the chain is the funnel, the brokerage is the business.
  • $MSTR. Sold 1,638 coins for roughly $105 million, raised $1 billion off the common at about one times net asset value, and spent $1.3 billion retiring converts. Per Apyx's Parker White, the dividend reserve went from six months back to about 18 and nothing puts until September 2027. The deleveraging is working.
  • $COIN. The legislative catalyst is priced at 20 percent for the year and industry volumes fell double digits last quarter. Jack Mallers frames the split honestly: Coinbase cares more about its own chain and alts than about Bitcoin. That is the bull case now, because the chains have the volume.

item.title: Galaxy lost $85 million and printed the best crypto earnings report of the cycle
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The Helios data centre billed its first rent and guided to $80 million a quarter at above 90 percent margins, while Mark Cuban sold most of his Bitcoin because the hedge did not hedge.
item.content:encoded:
The Helios data centre billed its first rent and guided to $80 million a quarter at above 90 percent margins, while Mark Cuban sold most of his Bitcoin because the hedge did not hedge.

Yesterday I said the miners had stopped being a Bitcoin trade. Galaxy Digital proved it with a net loss, a first rent cheque, and guidance that has nothing to do with the price of anything.

Market context. The Nasdaq rose more than 3 percent on the Hormuz route agreement Macro covers tonight. Bitcoin did not lead it, the fourth session running where the equities did the work.

Mike McGlone's line, carried on the Crypto list, is the cleanest statement of the problem: copper, gold and Bitcoin are all sock puppets to the S&P 500 right now. Gold at least got paid for it, up more than 4 percent above $4,300.

Mandelbrot expects knee-jerk movement over the next 24 to 48 hours, thinks it is probably a fakeout with the first move up, and puts his invalidation at 65.8. He has been pounding the table on the Nasdaq proxy over Bitcoin, and a 3 percent index day makes that uncomfortable rather than wrong.

The scoreboard.

  • Working. I moved to 60/40 yesterday that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. A fourth session of the equity complex ripping without it is the confirmation that call needs.
  • Confirmed the hard way. I have been carrying the Coldcard-drives-money-to-ETFs thread since Monday. Mark Cuban just sold most of his Bitcoin, and the reason was not custody.
  • Due within days. Galaxy's 830 megawatts at Helios needs a tenant, and the Texas queue that everything else depends on is now frozen.

1. Galaxy lost $85 million and the only number that mattered was $18.9 million. Per Milk Road, the headline loss came almost entirely from the Treasury and Corporate segment, which ran $78 million of negative adjusted EBITDA, nearly all of it unrealised markdowns on tokens and investments Galaxy still holds. Crypto fell in the quarter, so the book fell with it. That is beta, not a business.

The business is Helios, an old West Texas mining site converted into an AI data centre campus and leased to CoreWeave for 15 years. In Q2 it started charging rent.

Galaxy data centre segmentQ2
Leasing revenue$18.9 million, the first ever billed
Adjusted gross profit$20.1 million, from $3.1 million in Q1
Adjusted EBITDA$11.5 million, the first positive quarter ever
Phase I critical IT load in serviceall 133 MW
Guided Phase I billing from Q3roughly $80 million per quarter
Project-level adjusted EBITDA marginabove 90 percent

Their analyst wanted Q3 framed near $60 million and got $80 million. A 90 percent margin on contracted rent is a utility, worth a different multiple from anything that mines.

The crypto business held up better than crypto did. Digital Assets adjusted gross profit came in at $66 million, up 34 percent quarter over quarter, while Galaxy's own volumes fell 7 percent and industry volumes fell double digits. Galaxy also signed a multi-year staking agreement with BNY, a custodian overseeing more than $60 trillion.

2. Texas just froze the pipeline, and that makes the approved megawatts more valuable. This is the part with real consequence and almost nobody has priced it.

Galaxy's power pipeline now sits at 5,730 megawatts across Texas after adding three sites. Only 800 megawatts is contracted under an executed lease. The other 4,930 megawatts is identified but uncontracted, and most of it sits behind ERCOT's grid connection queue.

Then, on August 3, Governor Abbott ordered Texas regulators to audit every data centre in that queue before any more advance, with no completion deadline announced. ERCOT paused its Batch Zero study the same day.

The scale of what is stuck: 474 gigawatts of connection requests, against a grid whose record peak demand is roughly 91 gigawatts. Five times the entire peak load of Texas is sitting in a queue that just stopped moving.

That cuts two ways and the second way is the trade. It caps how fast anyone's pipeline can grow, which reprices every announced-but-unconnected megawatt in the state. And it makes the 830 megawatts already approved at Helios scarce in a way it was not last week.

Their analyst goes against his own readers and he is right to. Investors want the next tenant announced immediately. He thinks waiting gets better terms on a 15-year-plus lease, and with the queue frozen, time is on the landlord's side.

The dilution worry is sized. Every phase needs an equity cheque on top of the debt, and working back from Phase II terms he puts the requirement near $1 billion across all three phases against roughly $7 billion of levered free cash flow over the life of the leases, about a 35 percent return on committed equity.

3. Cuban sold because the hedge did not hedge. Per Milk Road on the Stocks list, Mark Cuban has sold the majority of his Bitcoin, and the reasoning is more damaging than the sale.

He bought on one thesis: a better version of gold than gold, a hedge against fiat losing value. Then the test arrived. During the Iran war, geopolitical risk spiked and the dollar slid, and Bitcoin fell while gold went to records. Bitcoin is priced in dollars, so a weaker dollar should have pulled global demand in. It did not.

He is reportedly more disappointed in Bitcoin than in Ethereum. Why this matters past one portfolio: the digital-gold framing is the backbone of institutional adoption. It is the reason pension funds, family offices and corporate treasuries started buying at all. If the hedge does not hedge in the one month it was asked to, the next marginal buyer at these prices needs a different reason, and nobody has supplied one.

Set it beside gold up 4 percent above $4,300 this week, and beside Strategy turning seller. The two largest structural arguments for owning Bitcoin, corporate treasury demand and the debasement hedge, both weakened inside five sessions. That is why I am comfortable at 60/40 even with the Nasdaq at a record.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $GLXY. An $85 million loss that is almost entirely paper markdowns, sitting on top of a data centre segment guiding to $80 million a quarter at above 90 percent margins. The three things to watch are whether Q3 leasing actually lands near $80 million, whether a Phase I refinancing appears, and whether the 830 megawatts finds a tenant.
  • $CRWV. The tenant on the other side of Galaxy's 15-year Helios lease, and the counterparty whose credit now underwrites someone else's utility economics. Its own numbers are worse than its landlord's, and that is the whole point of the split.
  • $MSTR. Sold 1,638 coins after four weeks of not buying, and Cuban's exit removes the narrative that made corporate treasuries buyers at all. Watch the premium to net asset value, because it decides whether the coins keep funding the coupon.
  • $IREN. Signed leases rather than hash, and now with the ERCOT queue frozen, already-approved capacity is the scarce asset. The Texas audit is a moat for whoever cleared it and a wall for everyone who did not.
  • $COIN. Macro has the CLARITY window closing with the recess on Saturday and no floor vote scheduled. Nothing today improved that, so the exchange keeps trading on volumes in a quarter when industry volumes fell double digits.

item.title: Strategy became a seller and Bitcoin sat out the best macro day in weeks
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Miners rallied 9.6 percent on data centre leases while Bitcoin finished flat against a Nasdaq up 1.4 percent, and the most reliable structural bid in the market spent last week selling.
item.content:encoded:
Miners rallied 9.6 percent on data centre leases while Bitcoin finished flat against a Nasdaq up 1.4 percent, and the most reliable structural bid in the market spent last week selling.

Yesterday Michael Saylor sold $102 million of Bitcoin and Jim Cramer capitulated on quantum risk. Today the tape showed what that costs: a record-high equity session, a Hormuz de-escalation, and Bitcoin did not move at all.

Market context. Per 0xResearch, Monday split the complex clean down the middle. Bitcoin was flat at negative 0.02 percent while the Nasdaq gained 1.4 percent and the S&P added 1.2.

The equities did all the work.

SectorMove
Crypto Miners+9.6 percent
Crypto Equities+4.5 percent
Modular+2.8 percent
DEXs-5.7 percent
Solana Eco-3.3 percent
Launchpad-2.9 percent

Token performance was fragmented rather than themed. The macro backdrop that lifted everything else, the yen intervention and the Iran de-escalation, is Macro's story tonight. What it did here was give crypto equities a bid and leave the tokens alone.

The scoreboard.

  • Working, and it is early. I went 55/45 yesterday that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. Flat on a day the Nasdaq rose 1.4 percent is the weak-tape confirmation that call needs, though nothing is settled.
  • Corroborated by two more names. I carried Anthony Pompliano's read that the Coldcard hack pushes money toward ETFs and third-party custody. Eric Balchunas and Dave Weisberger both landed independently in the same place today.
  • Resolved, and it is the one that matters. Strategy stopped being a buyer. After four weeks without a purchase it sold 1,638 Bitcoin last week to fund preferred dividends and STRC buybacks.

1. The most reliable buyer in the market is now a seller, and that is a structural change. Per 0xResearch, Strategy disclosed selling 1,638 Bitcoin last week to fund preferred dividends and STRC buybacks. That follows four straight weeks with no purchase at all.

Read it as plumbing rather than sentiment. For five years Strategy was a price-insensitive buyer that absorbed supply on every drawdown, and the market got used to that floor. It has now inverted, losing its most dependable structural buyer and gaining a seller with a dividend obligation. That is forced flow, and it does not care about your levels.

The mechanism does not reverse quickly. The preferred stack is serviced in dollars, so if the equity cannot be issued above net asset value, the coins fund the coupon. That treadmill speeds up as the discount widens.

I am moving to 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000, up from 55/45 yesterday. The upgrade is not about the macro, which improved today. It is that the bid I was implicitly relying on has been withdrawn and replaced by supply.

2. The miners are no longer a Bitcoin trade, and this week proved it. Twelve of the thirteen constituents are higher over the past week, and the leaders are not subtle.

MinerOne-week move
CIFR+24.9 percent
IREN+20.8 percent
HUT+19.3 percent

The driver is contracts rather than hash price. Per 0xResearch, IREN's $2.8 billion of AI-cloud deals and Hut 8's second $9.8 billion lease are still working through the sector. And per the Financial Markets list, Bitdeer jumped 23 percent on a 16-year AI and high-performance-computing data centre lease.

Sixteen years is the number to sit with. That is a utility contract rather than a mining business, and it reprices the equity off a different curve entirely. A miner with a signed decade-plus lease is a landlord.

So the sector has quietly split. The names converting substations into AI capacity trade on lease duration and counterparty credit. The ones still selling hash trade on Bitcoin, which went nowhere today. Own the first group and stop calling it a Bitcoin proxy.

3. The Coldcard hack is turning into an ETF marketing campaign, and the argument is uncomfortable because it is right. Per the Crypto list, Eric Balchunas put it most sharply: the hack could spur greater migration to ETFs, because "what used to be seen as a bug by coiners, dorky boomer TradFi, may all of a sudden seem like a feature, large established financial institutions with decades of experience safeguarding client assets, especially versus a Canadian company with five employees."

Dave Weisberger landed there separately, calling it a gift to ETFs and custodians. Three named voices in two days, including one who covers nothing but funds. Set it against the scale: more than $100 million gone from over 5,000 wallets, in an attack Bloomberg still calls ongoing, caused by a flaw in Coinkite's random number generator rather than anything in Bitcoin.

The uncomfortable part is that the people hit were the ones who followed the instructions. Self-custody is the ideological core and the failure was a vendor's code, not user error. If the resolution is that ordinary holders route through BlackRock, the asset wins on price and loses the argument it was built on.

4. The institutional plumbing kept building while the price did nothing. Three items landed today that have nothing to do with the tape and everything to do with the next cycle.

Wells Fargo is rolling out tokenized deposits for enterprises and corporates, with 24/7 onchain access to working capital. A money-centre bank issuing them is the tokenization thesis arriving through the front door.

Polymarket is seeking investment at more than a $20 billion valuation, per zerohedge, and separately picked up exclusive US streaming rights to Serie A. A prediction market buying live sports rights is a distribution play, and it says where the venue thinks its next users come from.

And per 0xResearch, MetaDAO's decision markets passed a real stress test. An attacker filed UMBRA-004 on July 31 seeking to move $1.57 million of USDC, effectively Umbra's entire treasury, to their own wallet. Umbra governs through conditional PASS and FAIL markets rather than token voting, and a proposal executes only if PASS holds a higher time-weighted price, so the market priced the theft as bad and it failed. Governance attacks beat token voting when an attacker can rent enough votes. Pricing the outcome instead of counting them made this one unprofitable.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MSTR. Sold 1,638 coins last week and has not bought in five. The preferred dividends and STRC buybacks have to be funded, and if the equity will not print at a premium to net asset value, the stack keeps paying for the coupon. Watch the premium, not the Bitcoin price.
  • $IREN. Up 20.8 percent on the week on $2.8 billion of AI-cloud deals. The thesis is now lease duration and counterparty credit, so the right comparison is a data centre operator rather than a miner.
  • $BTDR. Up 23 percent on a 16-year AI and high-performance-computing lease. Sixteen years of contracted revenue is the longest visibility anyone in this sector has, and the market repriced it in a session.
  • $COIN. Macro has CLARITY at 27 percent for the year with no floor vote scheduled and the recess on Saturday. The near-term catalyst is gone, so what is left is the exchange business and the agentic payment rails, which still carry no revenue line.
  • $HOOD. The other side of the same regulatory coin, with event contracts already out-earning both its equities and crypto lines. Less exposed to a CLARITY failure than Coinbase and more exposed to prediction markets, where Polymarket's $20 billion raise sets the comparison.
